en: So extending Pi and giving it new
capabilities with agent skills and prompt
templates is amazing. But
the true
killer feature of Pi, if you wanna call it
like this,
is its extensions support, which
allows you to add brand new features,
including changes to the UI of Pi, so how it
looks like in a terminal, or giving it new
tools by adding extensions. And with that, I
don't just mean that you can install
third-party packages, which we already did,
which use this mechanism under the hood, by
the way, but that you can also build your
own extensions locally on your system,
locally in a project, or globally on your
machine for all your PySessions.
And that you can, of course, also use Py to
build those extensions and extend itself,
basically. So you have self-improving
software, which is really just mind-blowing
and amazing.
And the idea is that you can use this
extensions feature, which you'll see in
action in just a second, to
add any kind of feature or behavior to Pi
you want, no matter if that is something
like permission gates, which we implemented
with help of a third-party package, which
under the hood used this extensions feature
to make sure that for certain commands, the
command is blocked until you approve it,
be that for other features like integrations
with external tools or services, or some
degrees of automation or whatever you want,
Pi Extensions got you covered because
through their Pi Extensions API, which is
built into Pi, which is supported by Pi, you
can listen
to all kinds of events that happen as Pi is
doing its work,
like when a session gets started or before
an agent gets started in a session, so
before it starts reacting or before a tool
is about to be executed. You can listen to
all these events and then run your own code
upon these events to change how Pi behaves
or what it's doing. So you could block a
tool execution, for example. You could
inject extra context whenever the agent
starts,
really whatever you want. And extensions can
change a lot of stuff. They can register new
tools, new slash commands, new shortcuts
even. They can also change the prompt or
inject extra context. They can change tool
calls, inject extra arguments or block them
or analyze the results and manipulate the
results of tool calls if you want to.
They can activate skills. They can also
change the UI and show dialogs or helper
messages inside of the terminal. All that is
supported by Py, which is
really, really amazing and useful. And of
course, as always, it's best to simply see
this in action here.
